lines.en: But not without a very special guest...
: I’m bored.
: Well, you had the opportunity to leave when that convoy of limos showed up, but you decided to follow me here instead. So you did this to yourself.
: Tsukasa Tsukioka deserves more than just a convoy of limos. If Mother thinks she can buy me off with just that, she is sorely mistaken.
: I can’t imagine buying you off at all is feasible considering how numb you already are to money at your age but, to satisfy my own curiosity, what will it take for you to leave?
: I’m making Mother come here to get me on her own. It isn’t fair that I should have to be surrounded by lowly peons on my own national holiday.
: I thought your mother was busy?
: She won’t be if I ask enough. That’s just how important I am.
In just seven hours, I have gone from the world’s most sexually active teacher to the world’s most exhausted teacher.
Well, after Wakana- who I’m consistently shocked to see roaming the halls despite looking like she is going to drop dead at any moment.
Regardless, I must now play babysitter while waiting for someone to come take this brat off of my hands.
I guess you can call it practice for when I have to visit Chika’s house and watch both her and Chinami soon, but at least then I’ll have Chinami to keep her occupied. And Touka to keep me occupied.
: Jeeves, tell me a story.
: No.
: But it’s-
: I know what day it is. But I will not be bossed around in my own office by someone I could pick up with one hand.
: If you’re not going to tell me a story, can you at least do something to keep me entertained?
: Like what?
: How am I supposed to know? You’re the adult here. Aren’t you supposed to be full of guidance and wisdom?
: I don’t think you’re old enough for my guidance and wisdom yet.
: What about that game you were playing with the peasant girl at the onsen?
: I really hope your mom gets here within the next thirty seconds because that is a road that even I am not ready to traverse just yet.
: Hah...Of course it’s not. This Tsukasa Day sucks. It’s like nobody is appreciating me any more than they normally do.
: The only difference is I got to go to high school. And even that wasn’t very fun.
: I’m not sure what you were expecting, but school isn’t really known for being “fun.”
: Not like I would know. I’m not allowed to go to school.
: Not allowed? Or just not willing to settle for a commoner school?
: I would settle for a commoner school if I had to.
: I’m the second in line to inherit the Tsukioka family business, so it’s not like I have to get the highest form of education when my older sister is going to be the one to take over.
: Unless staying here makes her brain turn into mush. Which, based on what I have seen here today, it might.
: While what you say may be true, I’m not really sure what that has to do with you not being allowed to go to school.
: Mother says I’m too “advanced” to go to school with girls my age and too young to go to school with Big Sister.
: So all I can do is sit at home and listen to boring old people talk about boring stuff when what I really want to do is have fun.
: I’ve been to your house. I have a hard time believing there isn’t anything fun to do there.
: Nothing’s really fun if you do it every day. Which is why I like going out and seeing other stuff that I’m not able to see at home. Like tacos. Or “the subway.”
: Or that very pale girl with the freckles who kept talking about demons.
: That’s Molly and she isn’t really a tourist destination.
: In fact, none of the things you listed are tourist destinations and you should probably do a little more research if you really want to see the outside world.
: Maybe.
: Or maybe you can officially accept the job as the new Jeeves Tsukioka the Thirteenth and we can go on all sorts of commoner adventures that-
: No.
: You are being very rude to me, Jeeves. This sort of behavior will not be tolerated.
: Fuck you.
: Ah! I’m telling Mother that you cursed at me!
: Do it. I’m pretty sure she’ll understand.
: Nuh-uh! Cursing at a child is something adults should never do! I’ve gotten at least ten other Jeeves fired because of that.
: If ten other Jeeves cursed at you, don’t you think the problem might be...I don’t know, you?
: Tsukasa Tsukioka isn’t a problem. She is gifted and talented and richer than you and everyone else you know combined.
: I know your sister, you know. And, unless she is a pathological liar who is only attending this school because she was excommunicated from your family, I’m pretty sure she’s rich too.
: She might as well be excommunicated with how often she talks about her new fun and exciting commoner life.
: It’s like she doesn’t even remember we’re better than you or something.
: Or...she’s just starting to realize you’re not?
: But we are.
: How?
: We’re smarter and cleaner and more sophisticated and cleaner and are trained in a variety of different skillsets that people like you aren’t exposed to. And also, we are cleaner.
: I don’t know where this strange fascination with our personal hygiene comes from, but there are plenty of people out here who are just as talented as you and Touka.
: Like Tsuneyo. She was a national kendo champion and now she is a...noodle warrior.
: A...noodle warrior?
: And then there’s Otoha who’s, like...some singing prodigy or something. And Nodoka, who is also prodigious in a lot of ways when she isn’t ruining the lives of ex-Yakuza.
: What about the one girl with the ponytail who kept glaring at you all day? What’s she really good at?
: Uhh...
: She’s good at...
: Eating?
: That doesn’t sound very impressive to me, Jeeves. If you were trying to make me realize how interesting you people can be, you should have stopped at the Yakuza part.
: The fact of the matter is that there’s just a lot more to what makes a person good than how talented they are or...how “clean” they are.
: Like what?
: Like how...nice they are. How open to change they are. How adaptable and versatile they can be in all types of situations.
: And who out of all of your students do you think is the best at all of those things?
: Touka.
: See, Jeeves? The Tsukioka family is just flat out better than everybody you know.
: Some members at least. Others...I’m not convinced yet. But sure, you win this round, Tsurumi.
: Of course I win! A Tsukioka does not pick losing battles. Not that there are many battles we’d lose in the first place, but still.
: You are easily the most prideful person I have ever met and you probably can’t even ride a bike yet.
: I don’t own a bike, but Big Sister lets me ride Morning Glory sometimes and I haven’t fallen off yet.
: Look at you, not even owning your own horse yet. And you call me a commoner.
: I own seven horses. They’re just all display pets.
: What good is a display horse?
: You’d know if you could afford one. But sadly, unless you accept my proposition and become a real Jeeves, you never will.
: How did you get like this when both of the other Tsukioka women are so approachable and kind?
: Some people are just born with the gift, I suppose.
: Is it too late to return it?
: When you’re as rich as Tsukasarumi Tsukioka, you don’t have to return anything. You can just buy something else.
: On second thought, I’m just going to blame your father as I can’t imagine Tsubasa or Touka having this sort of influence on you.
: It’s not Papa’s fault I’m like this. It’s probably just a side effect of being the second born in a family that typically only produces one heir.
: Besides, I don’t see him that much anyway. He’s always doing stuff and never has time for me anymore.
: Really? With how much you talk about him, I figured you bothered- err...I figured you were with him all the time.
: Not really. I try to talk to him as much as I can, but I think he forgets to charge his walkie talkie sometimes.
: Walkie talkie?
: Mhm. Santa brought me a walkie talkie a few years ago so I could talk to Papa whenever I wanted.
: Does he not have a cell phone?
: He does. But he says that it’s for work only and that I’m not allowed to call him on it during the day.
: I see...
: What do you spend most of your time at home doing then?
: Whatever I want. Drawing pictures. Swimming. Shifting all of Big Sister’s furniture that isn’t too heavy slightly to the left and watching her get confused.
: Oh, and getting the staff to do my bidding. Can’t forget about that. I have lots of bidding that needs to be done.
Her story reminds me of one I’m much closer to-
Of a girl who can barely speak about her father to me without the joy draining from her eyes as she slips into quiet reflection.
And while I feel I should be worrying that something like this may one day happen to Tsukasa as well-
Instead, I find myself wondering if Ayane saw the world through such unfortunate glass.
I’m sure that a lot of that is due to the fact that I just don’t really care about Tsukasa yet...but at least it helps me understand her.
It’s not at all unique for children to act out when they aren’t getting adequate attention from their parents after all.
But Tsukasa is still getting attention from one of her parents.
Maybe even a little too much attention if that parent is dropping what they’re doing just to come over here and pick them up despite a whole convoy of cars sent to do just that.
It’s just not the parent she wants, I guess.
: Tsukasa, dear...please tell me you are in there...
: About time, Mother. It’s been almost an hour and this room isn’t even climate controlled. And Jeeves is soooooo boring.
: Jeeves? But you fired Jeeves last- oh. Oh, Tsukasa! That is so rude for someone who’s done so much for our family in just a short while!
: All he’s done is get Big Sister to blab about him and the rest of her new friends all day long. Doesn’t that bother you?
: Not at all, dear. Your sister is finally-
: You know you can come in, right? You don’t have to talk through the door.
: Oh! Silly me. I probably would have stood there all day if you hadn’t said that.

: I’m terribly sorry for any trouble my youngest daughter may have caused you. I truly didn’t expect her to refuse all of our drivers when she knew I was busy, but...Tsukasa will be Tsukasa, I suppose.
: It’s National Tsukasa Day. I didn’t want to go home with someone being paid to care about me.
: But what about your sister? Couldn’t you have gone with her instead of burdening her teacher?
: Burden?
: It’s really no big deal. I’m usually here for an hour or two after class anyway. Tsukasa just sat on the couch.
: Tsukasa should have been a good girl and left school with one of the drivers like we agreed to this morning.
: But I wanted you.
: And you told me we could get ice cream after I finished my first day of high school to celebrate.
: Darling...that was when I assumed I didn’t have to take an hour away from my meetings just to come and get you.
: I’m not sure if we’ll have time anymore, dear.
: But...Tsukasa Day...
: Thank you again for watching over her, Sensei. I really do appreciate it.
: Yeah...no worries.
: Come along, dear. Sensei’s time is just as valuable as ours and we have taken up enough of it.
: Yes, Mother...
: Bye bye, Jeeves...
Tsukasa exits the office and...
And I somehow feel a little bad for her.
The feeling fades shortly after, though.
Things like that don’t normally last long for me.
But the fact that it came at all tells me she’s no longer just an arrogant waste of space in my mind.
She’s a girl, just like everyone else, trying to figure out how she best fits into this world.
And all things considered, that’s a lot better than just staying put and deciding you don’t belong at all.
